stops.name: Berlin, the Berliner Turnverein and the Turnfahrten
stops.campa: From the Hasenheide the thing spreads like wildfire. Jahn founds the Berliner Turnverein and leads the Turnfahrten: long marches into the country, hundreds of boys tramping in grey linen, singing, sleeping under the sky, camping like an army in training. To the fearful eyes of princes it looks like a secret host being raised; to Jahn it is exactly that. By the war's coming his gymnasts number in the hundreds, a brotherhood bound by the four words he gives them: frisch, fromm, fröhlich, frei.
stops.quote_source: Jahn's Turner motto, the four F's (Turnerkreuz)

stops.name: Breslau, the muster of the Free Corps
stops.campa: When Prussia rises at last against Napoleon in the spring of 1813, Jahn shuts the Turnplatz and marches. At Breslau the volunteer Free Corps of Major von Lützow is formed, and Jahn takes it up, leading a body of his older gymnasts into its ranks. Into the same black-clad corps come the poet Theodor Körner, the Turner Friesen, and the young Friedrich Fröbel, who leaves his crystals and his children's schoolroom to shoulder a musket. The Turnplatz has become an army; the training was always for this.

stops.name: Gadebusch, the wood where Körner falls
stops.campa: On 26 August 1813, in the wood of Rosenow near Gadebusch, the Lützowers clash with the enemy and the poet Theodor Körner is struck down, dying that same day with his sword-and-lyre songs unfinished. The corps that owes half its fame to his verse now owes it a martyr. Jahn marches on through the campaign with his gymnasts, the men he made strong on the Hasenheide now proving in blood what the leaping and vaulting were for. Lützow's wild hunt rides across the German north.
stops.quote: Das war Lützows wilde verwegene Jagd.

stops.name: The Göhrde, the charge and the maiden-soldier
stops.campa: On 16 September 1813 the Lützow corps fights at the Göhrde forest under Wallmoden, breaking French columns among the trees. Here Eleonore Prochaska, who marched disguised as the jäger August Renz, is torn by grapeshot carrying a wounded comrade from the line; only as her wounds are dressed is her sex discovered. She dies weeks later at Dannenberg, the maiden who bore arms for Germany. Around her the corps of gymnasts, poets and painters bleeds and holds: the flower of the awakening nation, forged and spent in a season.

stops.name: Leipzig, the Battle of the Nations
stops.campa: From 16 to 19 October 1813, on the fields around Leipzig, half a million men decide the fate of Europe in the Battle of the Nations, and Napoleon is broken and driven back over the Rhine. Jahn stands with the victory that answers, at last, the shame he swore upon at Jena seven years before. The bodies he trained have helped to free the fatherland. The Turnvater has kept his vow in arms; now he means to keep it in peace, raising a whole nation of such bodies for the Germany that must be made.

stops.name: Jena, the birth of the Urburschenschaft
stops.campa: On 12 June 1815 at Jena the returned volunteers found the first Burschenschaft, the German student brotherhood, in the colours black-red-gold that will one day be the nation's flag. Jahn's spirit is in it: his gymnasts and Lützowers are its founders, his gospel of one free Germany its creed. From the Turnplatz to the fraternity the same fire runs. The princes, restored and frightened, watch the students and the Turners with the same narrowing eye, sensing in this youth a power that means to unmake the map they have just redrawn.

stops.name: Berlin, Die Deutsche Turnkunst printed
stops.campa: In 1816 Jahn, with Ernst Eiselen, brings out Die Deutsche Turnkunst, the book that gives the movement its law. In it he sets down the apparatus and the exercises: the horse, the bars, the high bar, the vault; and the whole German tongue of Turnen he has forged, word by word, so that the leaping body might speak its own language. The laboriously rediscovered and awakened German gymnastic art, he writes, must not be marred by half-knowing. The scattered clubs now hold a single code; the master has written the scripture of the Turnplatz.
stops.quote: die mühsam wiedergefundene und erweckte deutsche Turnkunst
stops.quote_source: Friedrich Ludwig Jahn & Ernst Eiselen, Die Deutsche Turnkunst, Vorbericht (Berlin, 1816)

stops.name: Eisenach, the Wartburg: the students' fire
stops.campa: On 18 October 1817, on the fourth anniversary of Leipzig and the third centenary of Luther's theses, the Burschenschaften climb the Wartburg above Eisenach and light a great bonfire. As the songs and speeches rise, Jahn's men fling upon the flames mock-titles of reactionary books and the emblems of the old order: a corporal's cane, a Hessian pigtail-wig. Jahn is not present, yet the deed is laid at his door; the frightened courts read in the smoke of the Wartburg the shape of the demagogue they will now hunt. The reckoning is prepared.

stops.name: Berlin, the Turnplatz closed, the man taken
stops.campa: In March 1819 the student Karl Sand stabs the playwright Kotzebue, and the shot gives the princes their pretext. The Hasenheide is padlocked, the Turnen forbidden across the German lands: the Turnsperre that will bind the gymnasts for more than twenty years. On 13 July 1819 Jahn himself is arrested in Berlin as a demagogue, a stirrer of dangerous youth. The Father of Gymnastics, who freed his body for a fatherland, is marched off to prison by the very state whose armies he helped to victory. The open air is taken from him.

stops.name: Küstrin, the fortress on the Oder
stops.campa: From the Spandau citadel Jahn is moved to the fortress of Küstrin on the Oder, held while the courts pick over his words and his marches for treason they cannot quite find. He is questioned, transferred, kept: a body famous for leaping now shut behind casemate walls. The demagogue-hunt of the Karlsbad Decrees has found its most emblematic prisoner: the man who taught Germans to move, held motionless in a cell, while across the country the bars and beams of a hundred Turnplätze stand roped off and silent.

stops.name: Kolberg, the fortress by the Baltic
stops.campa: On 22 May 1820 Jahn is carried to the fortress of Kolberg on the Baltic, and there the long captivity grinds on. In 1823 his wife Helene dies, and he is not permitted to attend her funeral: the state denies the prisoner even his grief. He is tried, sentenced, the sentence quashed and renewed; his health frays behind the ramparts. For years the Turnvater sits by the cold sea, the freest of men in body made the most confined, paying with his own stillness for the movement he set loose upon Germany.

stops.name: Freyburg an der Unstrut, release under watch
stops.campa: On 15 March 1825 Jahn is freed at last, but on a leash: he may not live in any university or gymnasium town, and must report himself to the police. He settles in the little wine-town of Freyburg on the Unstrut, marries Emilie Hentsch, and builds a house there, a watched pensioner, forbidden his own life's work. Among the vineyards the caged Turnvater grows old, receiving pilgrims who steal to his door, the living monument of a banned movement, waiting out the fear of princes with the patience of stone.
